summary: Extends the URL MIME External-Body access type so any MIME part of a SIP message can be referred to indirectly by a URI. This meets the content indirection requirements of SIP. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: Some SIP messages carry content that is too big for the signaling path, or that lives on another server. This document lets a sender put a web address in the message instead of the content itself. The receiver then fetches the content over HTTP or another protocol, and can decide from the address and its parameters whether it is worth fetching.

questions: mime part referenced by uri in sip
how does sip reject content indirection
subtitle: How a SIP message can point to a body part by URI instead of carrying it, using the message/external-body type.

tldr.problem: SIP is not a general data transport, and large or remote content can overload signaling proxies, strain slow links or live somewhere other than on the endpoint.
tldr.mechanism: A SIP body part is replaced by a message/external-body part that names a URI, with parameters for expiry, size and hash and headers for type, purpose and version. The receiver fetches the content over HTTP or another protocol.
tldr.outcome: Any MIME part of a SIP message can be sent indirectly, and the receiver can decide whether to fetch it. Security relies on screening URIs, S/MIME and an optional SHA-1 hash.

today: RFC 4483 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2006. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on RFC 2017, which defines the external-body access type it extends, and on RFC 3261, which defines SIP itself.

sections.title: Purpose and the Gap It Fills
sections.content:
The purpose of the Session Initiation Protocol, defined in RFC 3261, is to create, modify or terminate sessions with one or more participants. SIP messages, like HTTP messages, are syntactically composed of a start line, one or more headers and an optional body. Unlike HTTP, SIP is not designed as a general-purpose data transport protocol.

The document gives several reasons for specifying the content of a SIP message body indirectly. For bandwidth-limited applications such as cellular wireless, indirection lets the sender annotate the content with metadata that the recipient can use to decide whether to retrieve the content over a resource-limited link. The size of the content might otherwise overwhelm intermediate signaling proxies and unnecessarily increase network latency, which can be unacceptable for time-sensitive SIP applications; indirect content moves the transfer out of the SIP signaling network and into a potentially separate data transfer channel. The session-related data may also not reside on the endpoint or user agent at all, in which case the message can carry an indirect reference that the receiver resolves over a non-SIP transfer channel such as HTTP, FTP or LDAP.

The purpose of content indirection is purely to provide an alternative transport mechanism for SIP MIME body parts. Apart from the transport mechanism, indirect body parts are equivalent to inline body parts and should get the same treatment.

Earlier attempts at the problem used the text/uri-list MIME type, a list of URIs delimited by end-of-line markers. It failed to satisfy the requirements for a general-purpose content indirection mechanism in SIP, most notably because it cannot specify attributes on a per-URI basis, such as version information or the MIME type of the referenced content.

RFC 2017 defines an extension to the message/external-body MIME type originally defined in RFC 2046. The extension allows a generic URI to specify the location of the content, instead of the protocol-specific parameters for FTP and others that RFC 2046 defined. It provides most of the functionality needed, but by itself it is not a complete solution, so this document specifies how to use it.

The requirements are divided into those that apply to the URI, which indirectly references the content, and those that apply to the content itself. Where possible, existing MIME parameters and entity headers are used: MIME Content-Type parameters are the preferred way to describe the URI, and entity headers are the preferred way to describe the indirect content.
sections.plainLanguage: SIP messages carry headers and sometimes a body, but SIP was not built to move bulk data. This document lets a sender replace a body part with a pointer to a URI. The receiver fetches the content itself, over HTTP or another transfer protocol, and treats the fetched part exactly as it would treat an inline one.

sections.title: Use Cases: Presence Notification and Document Sharing
sections.content:
The first example is presence notification. The information carried in a presence document can exceed the recommended size for a SIP NOTIFY request, particularly when the document aggregates information from multiple endpoints. In that case the NOTIFY request can carry an indirect pointer to the presence document, which the watcher then retrieves over HTTP. The exchange runs like this: the watcher sends SUBSCRIBE to the presence server and receives a 200 OK; the server sends a NOTIFY with the document inline and the watcher replies 200 OK; the server then sends a NOTIFY with a URI and the watcher replies 200; the watcher then issues an HTTP GET and receives application/cpim-pidf+xml.

The second example is document sharing during an instant messaging conversation. One party sends a MESSAGE request with an indirect pointer to a document that the remote party should render. Carrying the document directly in the MESSAGE request is not an appropriate use of the signaling channel, and the document may live on a completely independent server from that of the party sending it. In the example a user agent client wants to exchange a JPEG image that she has stored on her web server with a user agent server she is talking to, and intends to render the JPEG inline in the conversation. The recipient of the MESSAGE request launches an HTTP GET request to the web server to retrieve the JPEG image.
sections.plainLanguage: Two situations are given. A presence document that is too large for a NOTIFY message can be pointed at instead, so the watcher fetches it with an HTTP GET. In a chat, a picture that lives on a web server can be sent as a pointer, and the recipient fetches it there rather than inside the chat message.

sections.title: Requirements
sections.content:
The document lists what the mechanism has to be able to do. It MUST be possible to specify the location of content via a URI, and such URIs MUST conform with RFC 2396. It MUST be possible to specify the length and the type of the indirect content, and to specify the disposition of each URI independently.

It MUST be possible to label each URI to say whether and when the content it refers to has changed, so that the receiver can tell without retrieving the content. The examples given for a label are a sequence number, a timestamp and a version number; with HTTP, the entity-tag mechanism in RFC 2068 may be appropriate. What is labelled is the content, not the URI itself, so the label is effectively metadata of the content. It MUST also be possible to specify the time span for which a given URI is valid, which may or may not be the same as the lifetime of the content itself.

It MUST be possible for both sides to indicate support for the mechanism, and a fallback mechanism SHOULD be specified for the case where one party cannot support content indirection. It MUST be possible to negotiate the type of the indirect content, and separately to negotiate support for any URI scheme to be used. It SHOULD be possible to ensure the integrity and confidentiality of the URI when it is received. The content indirection MUST be processable without human intervention, and it MUST be possible to transfer content indirectly in any SIP message that would otherwise carry that content as a body.
sections.plainLanguage: The requirements ask for a pointer that says where the content is, how big it is, what type it is and what to do with it. The pointer also has to say when it stops working and how to tell whether the content behind it has changed. Both sides have to be able to say that they support the mechanism, and the whole thing must work without asking a human first.

sections.title: Applying RFC 2017 to the Requirements
sections.content:
A user agent client or server indicates support for content indirection by including the message/external-body MIME type in its Accept header, and MAY add values naming the content types it is willing to accept, either directly or through content indirection. A user agent that supports content indirection MUST support indirection of the application/sdp MIME type.

Applications that use the mechanism MUST support the HTTP URI scheme, and a user agent MUST support receiving an HTTP URI for indirect content if it advertises support for content indirection. A user agent server MAY advertise alternative access schemes in the schemes parameter of the Contact header, as described in RFC 3840.

The URI for the indirect content is given in a URL parameter of the message/external-body MIME type, and an access-type parameter says that the external content is referenced by a URI. The HTTP URI specifications MUST conform to RFC 2396.

Content that is not critical to the context of the communication can be marked optional, using the Critical-Content mechanism described in RFC 3459. If the user agent server is unable to fetch or render an optional body part, it MUST NOT return an error to the user agent client.

To let the receiver tell whether the content behind a URI has changed, a Content-ID entity header is used. Changes in the underlying content MUST result in a change in the Content-ID associated with that URI, and multiple SIP messages that carry URIs for the same content SHOULD reuse the same Content-ID so the receiver can cache the content and avoid unnecessary retrievals. The Content-ID is intended to be globally unique and SHOULD be temporally unique across SIP dialogs.

The URI is not required to stay valid for an indefinite period, so the supplier of the URI MUST specify the period for which it is valid and accessible. This is done with an EXPIRATION parameter of the Content-Type header, whose value is an RFC 1123 date-time restricted to GMT time, consistent with the Date header in SIP. The parameter is mandatory, and the date-time value can range from minutes to days or even years.

To support the existing SIP mechanisms for negotiating content types, a Content-Type entity header SHOULD be present in the entity itself. If the protocol of the URI supports its own content negotiation mechanisms, such as HTTP, that header may be omitted. The sender MUST be prepared for the receiving party to reject content indirection if the receiver cannot negotiate an appropriate MIME type using the underlying protocol of the URI scheme.

When the size of the indirect content is known in advance, a size parameter on the Content-Type header SHOULD be supplied, in bytes. This is an extension of RFC 2017 that is in line with the other access types defined for message/external-body in RFC 2046, and it helps the receiver decide whether to retrieve the content. As with directly supplied content, a user agent server may return a 513 error response if the content size is too large. The size parameter is optional. A Content-Disposition entity header MUST be present for all indirect content, and it states the purpose of the content. The Content-Description entity header MAY carry optional freeform text commenting on the content; it may be shown to the end user but MUST NOT be used by other elements to determine the disposition of the body.

If several URIs are needed, an appropriate multipart MIME type should be used, with each URI contained in a single entity, and indirect content may be mixed with directly supplied content, which is particularly useful with multipart/alternative. The document does not change the meaning of the multipart flavors, particularly multipart/related as described in RFC 2387.
sections.plainLanguage: The reference travels in a Content-Type header of type message/external-body. The URL parameter holds the address, expiration says when it stops working, and size says how many bytes to expect. A Content-ID marks which version of the content is meant, a Content-Type says what it is, and a Content-Disposition says what to do with it. An optional hash parameter lets the receiver check that the content is exactly what the sender meant.

sections.title: Rejection, Optional Content and Fallbacks
sections.content:
If a user agent server receives a SIP request that contains a content indirection payload and cannot or does not wish to support that content type, it MUST reject the request with a 415 Unsupported Media Type response. The user agent client can tell the two cases apart from the Accept header of the response: the absence of the message/external-body MIME type means the server does not support content indirection at all, and the absence of the particular MIME type of the requested content means the server does not support that media type.

Where the content is not critical to the communication, the mechanism marks it optional, and the server then returns no error if it cannot fetch or render that part. Where the mechanism itself is not supported by the other party, the requirements call for a fallback mechanism to be specified.

SIP defines three headers, Call-Info, Error-Info and Alert-Info, that supply additional information about a session, an error response or alerting. All three let the user agent client or server point at additional information with a URI, so they can be considered a form of content indirection. This mechanism is not intended as a replacement for them. Where they apply, the SIP headers MUST be used in preference, because of their well-defined semantics.
sections.plainLanguage: A server that cannot handle the referenced content rejects the request with a 415 Unsupported Media Type response, and the response tells the sender why. Content that does not matter to the conversation can be marked optional, so a failure to fetch it causes no error. The Call-Info, Error-Info and Alert-Info headers already point at extra information, so they are preferred over this mechanism.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Any content indirection mechanism introduces additional security concerns, because it needs an extra processing step and an extra information transfer. The document lists four possible abuses. The initiator can choose an alternative protocol with weaker security or known vulnerabilities for the content transfer, for example by asking the recipient to make an HTTP request that results in a Basic authentication challenge. The initiator can ask the recipient to consume additional resources in the transfer and in content processing, which can create a route for denial-of-service attacks, for example an active FTP URL that consumes two connections for every indirect content message. The indirection can be used as a form of port scanning, where the indirect content URL is a bogus URL pointing at an internal resource of the recipient, and the response to the request reveals information about open and vulnerable ports there. And an indirection URL can disclose sensitive information about the initiator, such as an internal user name in an HTTP URL or possibly geolocation information.

The document says all of these can be mitigated through careful screening of both the indirect content URIs that are received and those that are sent, and that integrity and confidentiality protection of the URI can prevent additional attacks. For confidentiality, integrity and authentication, the mechanism relies on the security mechanisms of RFC 3261, and in particular the use of S/MIME as defined in Section 23 of RFC 3261, which provides the necessary protection for the indirect content URI and its associated parameters.

Securing the transfer of the indirect content is the responsibility of the protocol used for that transfer. If HTTP is used, applications SHOULD support the HTTPS URI scheme and MUST support upgrading connections to TLS with starttls. A failure to complete HTTPS or starttls, for example because of a certificate or encryption mismatch, after the indirect content has already been accepted in the SIP request is not the same as rejecting the SIP request, and it may need extra communication between the two users to correct.

The document does not advocate transitive trust: just because the server received a URI from a client it trusts, the server SHOULD NOT implicitly trust the object the URI refers to without establishing its own trust relationship with the provider of that object. Access control to the referenced content is not defined by the document; the protocol for the scheme of the URI may define it.

If the sender knows the content in advance, it SHOULD include a hash parameter, a hexadecimal-encoded SHA-1 hash of the indirect content. When a hash is included, the recipient MUST check the indirect content against it and indicate any mismatch to the user. When the hash parameter is included and the target URI involves setting up a security context with certificates, the server MUST ignore the results of the certificate validation procedure and instead verify that the hash of the canonicalized content received matches the hash in the parameter. When the hash parameter is not included, the sender SHOULD use only schemes that offer message integrity, such as https, and the server MUST verify any server certificates using its list of trusted top-level certificate authorities. Without hashing, the content returned to the recipient might have been altered from what the sender intended.
sections.plainLanguage: A pointer can be abused. The sender can pick a weaker protocol, make the receiver fetch a lot of data, aim the pointer at an internal host to find out which ports are open, or leak information about itself in the address. The document therefore requires screening of the URIs on both sides, protection of the URI with S/MIME, and an optional SHA-1 hash of the content that the receiver must check.

viz.caption: THE PARAMETERS AND HEADERS THAT CARRY THE REFERENCE

items.title: URL parameter
items.text: The URI that locates the indirect content. Required.

items.title: expiration parameter
items.text: The date and time in GMT after which the URI is no longer valid. Required.

items.title: size parameter
items.text: The size of the indirect content in bytes. Optional.

items.title: hash parameter
items.text: A hex-encoded SHA-1 hash of the content, for the receiver to check.

items.title: Content-ID
items.text: Marks which version of the content the URI points at.

items.title: Content-Type
items.text: The MIME type of the indirect content.

items.title: Content-Disposition
items.text: The purpose of the content. Required for all indirect content.

items.title: Accept header
items.text: How a user agent says it supports content indirection.

data.title: An INVITE with indirect content
data.code:
INVITE sip:boromir@example.com SIP/2.0
From: <sip:gandalf@example.net>;tag=347242
To: <sip:boromir@example.com>
Call-ID: 3573853342923422@example.net
CSeq: 2131 INVITE
Accept: message/external-body application/sdp
Content-Type: message/external-body;
     ACCESS-TYPE=URL;
     URL="http://www.example.net/party/06/2002/announcement";
     EXPIRATION="Sat, 20 Jun 2002 12:00:00 GMT";
     size=231
Content-Length: 105

Content-Type: application/sdp
Content-Disposition: session
Content-ID: <4e5562cd1214427d@example.net>
